paper_summary: Kitahara, Akiyama and Ueno (Journal of Japan Institute of Light Metals, 40(12), 1990, in Japanese) study a metal-matrix syntactic foam, 'SBAC', made of Shirasu Balloons (SB - volcanic hollow glass microballoons, specific gravity 0.563, 149-210 um) in an Al-12%Si casting alloy (AC3A). The SB volume fraction VSB was varied from 0 to 60 vol% by packing SB together with 149-490 um Al-12%Si alloy powder into a die and pressure-infiltrating molten Al-12%Si into the interstices. Tensile strength, compressive strength, shear modulus, internal friction coefficient and electrical conductivity were measured against VSB: shear modulus fell exponentially and monotonically and followed a logarithmic mixture rule (Kerner and Takano models did not fit), while tensile strength, compressive strength and conductivity fell exponentially with a sharp downward knee near 50 vol% and internal friction rose linearly with a sharp upward knee at the same point, attributed to a rapid increase in SB-SB contact points above the loosest cubic packing fraction (52.4 vol%).

extraction_notes:
MAJOR CAVEAT: this 1990 Japanese-language paper reports the whole VSB dependence graphically only. Tensile strength and compressive strength vs VSB (Fig. 1 and the log-log Fig. 5), shear modulus and internal friction vs VSB (Fig. 2) and specific conductivity vs VSB (Fig. 3) carry no numeric values in the text and there is no data table for the composites. The only property values stated numerically anywhere in the text are those of the SB-free matrix baseline (VSB = 0). Therefore NO record could be created for any actual SB-containing composition, even though the study covers VSB = 0-60 vol%; reading values off the figures is not permitted. The three records here are all the VSB = 0 matrix baseline, one per test type (tension, compression, torsion/shear).

The paper is definitely on-topic: SBAC is an Al-12%Si matrix syntactic foam filled with hollow volcanic glass microballoons (Shirasu Balloons), made by pressure infiltration of molten alloy into a die pre-packed with SB plus 149-490 um Al-12%Si alloy powder.

DERIVED VALUES (flagged, not stated verbatim in the paper):
- particle_mean_diameter_um = 179.6 um, from the stated mean particle RADIUS R = 89.8 um (x2). Size range given as 149-210 um diameter.
- particle_wall_thickness_ratio = 0.9422, computed as eta = (R - h)/R from the stated R = 89.8 um and measured wall thickness h = 5.19 um.
- strain_rate_per_s: the paper gives only the crosshead speed (8.33 um/s, identical for tension and compression). Nominal rates were computed as speed / specimen length: 8.33e-3 mm/s / 15 mm parallel length = 5.55e-4 1/s (tension) and / 20 mm height = 4.17e-4 1/s (compression). Both are quasi-static.

UNIT / TYPO NOTES: 'G=27.4Pa' in the results paragraph is a typo for 27.4 GPa (confirmed by the later sentence using 'the measured value 27.4 GPa'); recorded as 27400 MPa. The internal friction coefficient Q^-1 = 0.0040 is mapped to loss_tangent (Q^-1 = tan delta). SB specific gravity 0.563 is used as particle_true_density_g_cc.

NOT REPRESENTABLE IN THE SCHEMA: electrical conductivity of the matrix, C = 8.40 MS/m (and the whole conductivity-vs-VSB curve), has no schema field and is not recorded. Compressive strength for VSB <= 10 vol% is a 0.2% proof stress, not a peak stress (footnote *1).

MODEL / CONSTITUENT VALUES NOT MADE INTO RECORDS (they are properties of the balloons or the glass, not of a composite specimen): apparent bulk modulus of SB KSB = 3.45 GPa; apparent shear modulus of SB GSB estimated as 2.38 GPa (elastic relation), 3.15 GPa (Takano model), 3.44 GPa (log mixture-rule least-squares fit, eq. 4) - note the conclusions section instead quotes GSB = 2.63 GPa and Gm = 27.4 GPa, which is inconsistent with the 27.2 / 3.44 GPa pair given in eq. (4) in the body; Shirasu glass wall properties calculated from oxide composition, ESG = 69.9 GPa, GSG = 28.6 GPa, nu_SG = 0.22. Kerner's and Takano's mixture rules were both found not to fit; the empirical logarithmic mixture rule log G = (1-VSB) log Gm + VSB log GSB fitted well.
